utterances.text: Well, then, will you please tell us: In your statement that you gave to the investigators, you mentioned that Zoran Vokic was wearing a gold earring in his right ear, in the form of a cross. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what it says in my statement, then it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember, when this beating occurred, what did that person use to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to go back to that again? I've gone into all that once. Do I really have to? I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have to answer questions put to you. If you can remember, you say so. You tell us what you remember. If you can't remember, you simply say, "I can't remember." That is an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. You're quite right. To avoid this further torture, I can't remember those things, and I don't want to go into them. It was the worst situation for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, if you can't remember. Is it true, what you told the investigators, that that person beat you with an iron rail and a rubber truncheon with a spring and a ball at the end of it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blows were terrible. I'm talking in general terms. They beat me with a rubber truncheon and with that spring which had a ball at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have no further questions. I apologise, Your Honour. We have no further questions but we would like to tender the statement -- or perhaps we can do that at the end. I'm sorry. We have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that no positive identification of my client was made, we will have no questions. But if this identification, any attempt is made to accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, you can ask questions or not ask questions. You cannot make that conclusion as to whether there was a positive identification or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was no positive identification, as has been entered in the record by the Prosecution, so we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now move on to any additional questions. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, on cross-examination you were asked some questions about who was responsible for prisoners and prisons. I would ask you, sir, did the Prijedor Police Department have cells in which it held people who had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had one cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were the police officers belonging to the police department those who were responsible for those prisoners in that cell?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were also asked questions about a duty officer or an operative duty officer, and you testified you did not know what was meant by that.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a position called "shift leader"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that position?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That position was an authorised official who was at the head of the operative affairs of the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the duties of that individual?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person would send workers to work; that person was constantly in radio communication with the workers, officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many shift leaders would be on duty at any one particular time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked within a system of two first shifts, two second shifts, and two third shifts, and then two days off, and so according to that system, four persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So a shift leader in charge of each shift.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked questions about an incident at Hambarine, and it was indicated that people there were killed as a result of that incident. Did you speak with anyone who was wounded as a result of that incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ferid Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony on direct examination, you talked about a person named Ferid Sikiric. Is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you talked to this Ferid Sikiric, did he tell you how he was injured?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the time at a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At which checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hambarine checkpoint. A vehicle came from the direction of Prijedor, moving in the direction of Ljubija. According to well-founded suspicions and some information received that the vehicle was transporting weapons in fact, the vehicle was stopped for a search and control to be conducted. The driver of the vehicle stopped his vehicle. Another person who was at the checkpoint approached to see what was going on. Everybody was asked to leave the vehicle. At that moment the person who was sitting behind the driver, through the door, that is to say, from inside the car, he opened fire through the door of the vehicle. Ferid Sikiric was hit. The second individual, that is to say, the third individual, the person who could see the car, responded to the fire and shot in turn, returned fire. That's how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, at one point in cross-examination you were being asked about your interrogations, and you were asked if any people who had worked in the Prijedor Police Station ever took part in interrogating you. You answered that Nenad Lakic took part in that, and it appeared that you had other names you wished to give but you were interrupted. Do you recall anyone else from the Prijedor Police Station who was present when you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nebojsa Tomicic and another Nebojsa; we had two Nebojsas. I was interrogated in their presence and we had to sign some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Other than those individuals, do you recall the names of any personnel from the Prijedor Police Station who were present when you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, during my first interrogation, the chief of the crime department, Ranko Ivic [as interpreted], and there was something that was brought into question and I asked him to confirm my story.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would you give that name again? Who was the chief of the crime department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked some questions about a document, document 17/1, and you were referred to paragraph 7, the sentence which indicated that the mine's management would organise meals for detainees in conjunction with the quartermaster corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the document it says the mine's management of Ljubija, not the management of the camp, which was the interpretation we got. I don't know what Ms. Hollis said but it says, the mine's management of Ljubija, the Ljubija mine's management and not the camp management. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what I intended to say. I'm not sure I said that. But anyway, I certainly did not mean to say Ljubija and I don't believe I did, so perhaps the interpretation could be clarified. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, may I ask you, when did you first receive food in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about four or five days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were held in the camp, did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question was not raised in the cross-examination by any of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was asked about the paragraph assigning responsibility for organising food in the camp; my questions are relevant to that. The Prosecution would suggest the inference which the Defence will wish to be drawn from that is that the mine's management was responsible for any difficulties with food. We are exploring that situation with these questions. We believe that it is relevant to the cross-examination and we would ask to be allowed to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to give the floor to Mr. Simic to know whether he agrees with the response made by Ms. Hollis, whether you accept -- let me correct myself, whether you accept what Ms. Hollis has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not accept what Ms. Hollis has said because the object of our cross-examination was who was responsible; that is to say, we wanted to show the system of organisation and the functioning of the camp and not the method of providing food. We discussed that at length with other witnesses. This particular witness did not speak about that during his testimony, during his examination-in-chief and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber considers that you have opened the question of meals, which was included in the document, and therefore Ms. Hollis can ask her question. Before you continue, Ms. Hollis, I would like to hear Mr. O'Sullivan. He had an objection to make, I think. Mr. O'Sullivan was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My objection is that the test for whether or not re-examination is possible it is not, as Ms. Hollis suggests, whether her questions are relevant. Relevancy is not the issue. In my submission, re-examination is limited to questions raised during cross-examination which are unclear, which require clarification. There's no ambiguity in the questions put to this witness during the cross-examination, nor in his answers. This is an attempt to engage in examination-in-chief, which is not permitted during re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan, but the question of meals, of food, was an essential question to this case, and therefore -- just one moment, please, for me to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, you may continue with the question. The Chamber feels that it comes within the scope of the regulations. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, during your detention in Omarska, did you receive food every day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any camp personnel ever intervene to ensure that you received food?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you were also questioned about paragraph 7 of this same document as it related to the mines' management organising regular cleaning and maintenance. Were there regular cleaning and maintenance of the areas where you were detained in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any camp personnel ever intervene to ensure that the areas where you were held were regularly cleaned and maintained?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During cross-examination by Defence counsel for accused Radic, you were asked about locations where Radic was during times that people were called out. I would ask you to assist the Court, please, and tell the Court in what different locations did you see the accused Radic when people were called out? You have mentioned one such location. I would ask you to assist the Court and tell them the other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was listening to the interpretation, thus the lag. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you said that we should not repeat questions that have already been asked. I posed exactly the same question in the same word order, but I didn't insist upon it because of your advice. You advised otherwise. Now, does the witness only answer the Prosecution and not us? So I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, your response to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the general rule is that you don't repeat questions that were asked and answered. This question is being repeated because it was not answered. Your Honours are free to determine the significance of the fact that it was not answered for Defence counsel for Mr. Radic, and whether it is answered when I ask it, and why that may be. But it was not answered, and that's why I'm asking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, please go ahead. I do apologise. You know, there is always a slight delay because I'm listening to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was given that Mladjo Radic was at different places, depending on the situation. I asked twice, I got the same answer twice. And I don't understand what Ms. Hollis wants, apart from getting something else. That is what the witness answered twice, so why go into it a third time? And I still maintain that questions should not be repeated in order to get a different answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, please don't repeat the question, but you can, of course, specify and go on, go into specifics, and reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll attempt to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will attempt to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On cross-examination by Defence counsel for accused Radic, you indicated that in addition to the rounded area on the administration building, that you saw accused Radic present in different locations when people were called out. Could you please assist the Court and specify where those different locations were.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In addition to what I've already stated, the locations were here in this building, on this model, which means in the building, the space referred to as maintenance, where cars were maintenanced, repaired. That's where we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you're talking about "this building," could you tell us how that building was referred to by the detainees? What was the building called?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maintenance building, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your direct testimony you mentioned the repair building and you said that was the hangar building.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is the maintenance building the same as the repair building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were also asked questions on cross-examination based upon a statement that you had given, and you were asked questions in regard to a person called Vokic and how you had described Vokic. At this time I would like to show you what I will mark as Exhibit 3/98A, being the English, and B being the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And I would ask that this statement be provided to the witness. And I also have copies for Your Honours. And if any Defence counsel do not have a copy of this statement, it is dated 27, 28, 29 April 1995. If anyone needs it, I have that for them. Would you give them both copies, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask that you first look at 3/98A, and I would ask you, if you look at the first page of that statement, does your signature appear on the first page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you look at pages 2, 3, 4, and 5, and 6, does your signature appear on each page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall giving this statement to members of the Prosecution in April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And at that time did you answer questions to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you answer questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this statement read back to you in a language you understood before you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The statement was not read to you in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will pull the statement back, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then, sir, tell us: How is it you were able to say that the statement was accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I -- I can't say. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Perhaps the witness is confusing this with another statement that we discussed here. Ms. Hollis, could you be more specific? But I see Mr. Fila on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis said that she withdraws the statement. If she said that, then I don't think we can continue discussing that statement, if she has withdrawn it. That is my opinion. So why should we go on asking about something that has been withdrawn? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when Ms. Hollis asked you the question and wanted to know whether before signing this paper that you have in front of you, the paper before you, did somebody read to you in your language that statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just signed the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before signing the English version -- there we are. You have in front of you -- have you got a B/C/S version in front of you, the document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ELMO -- no, we've got nothing on the ELMO. Never mind. So what you are telling us is that you signed the English version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't understand English, I take it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before signing, did somebody translate for you what was written in English?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Yes, but not in written form, not in writing. That's where the misunderstanding arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, tell me one more time so that we understand things clearly: Before signing the English version, did somebody translate orally for you and then you signed? Is that how it happened, or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with that clarification, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment. I see Mr. O'Sullivan has an objection to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just a matter of clarification. We now have testimony that he did not have it read back to him in a language he understood, and now he says he did. So you put the same question to the witness as Ms. Hollis. He's answered differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No basis to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, if I heard the witness correctly, he said that he did not sign the B/C/S version; he signed the English version. Before signing, nobody gave him a translation, but did the oral translation for him, and, having had that oral translation, he signed. Is that clear, or are there still any obscure points? And the transcript speaks for itself, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's precisely my point, Your Honour. On page 69 of LiveNote, line 15, the question from Ms. Hollis is this: "Was this statement read back to you in a language you understand before you signed the statement?" Answer: "No." Next question: "The statement was not read to you in a language you understand?" Answer: "No." That's the basis for my arguing that this statement should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, to withdraw the statement, why? I began my intervention admitting the possibility that the witness was not clear on what declaration was meant, and I admitted that, in fact, he did have an English version on the ELMO and a B/C/S version in front of him. Having clarified that, the witness was clear in saying that before signing the English version, he received an oral translation in B/C/S, so he could know what he was about to sign, and therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't take the point much further other than to say he had the document in front of him when Ms. Hollis originally put her questions to him. So in my submission, there was no confusion in the mind of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said to Madam Hollis that she could continue, it was to continue her response. I think it is now quite clear from the transcript, so you may continue, Ms. Hollis, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would simply have one more question related to this statement, related to the issue of the objection. I would ask that the witness look at the last page of the B/C/S, which should be page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Witness, the last page of the B/C/S, please, page 7. Page 7, please, if you would turn it to the last page of the B/C/S. The last page of the B/C/S, "Witness Acknowledgement." Do you see that, sir? Does it state: "This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection"? Does it say that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the bottom of that acknowledgement, does your signature appear?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where it says "Signed," is that your signature? If you would look again at the English, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Does your signature appear on the English statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, just to make it absolutely clear, are you now telling the Court that the statement was read to you in the Bosnian language and you certified that it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at this statement in the Bosnian language --

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- does this statement refer to the beating by Tadic and the presence of a man you identify as Vokic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that came subsequently, but I would have to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you look at the statement and see if the statement includes information about a man you identify as Vokic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you look at page 6 of the Bosnian language version --

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- does that indicate that you did not know Vokic from before?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said today, earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That another person --

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- indicated Vokic.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj, I have only a couple of questions. Apart from the information you got from the security guard whose name you do not wish to reveal publicly -- leave that aside -- what, if any, other indications did you have while you were in the camp that Mr. Kvocka had a role as a superior?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What, if any, other indications? Leave the information out that you got from your security guard. Would you just tell us how, if you did, you came to the conclusion that he was some sort of, you used the word, "boss," in your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the indications was that the detainees were talking -- I wasn't present -- that he had addressed a group of detainees and introduced himself as the camp commander. Then another version, mine: I could note by the behaviour and situation in the camp, when the shifts were changing, when the bus would arrive with the new shift and while it was standing parked, the shift leaders would be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My second question is: You also said that you saw Mr. Kvocka, I believe, early on in the presence of Mr. Meakic at one point, is that right, in the camp? Is that what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Later on you said that Mr. Meakic was the commander up till two weeks before the camp disbanded in August. How were you able to tell when, in your impression, Mr. Kvocka was the commander and when Mr. Meakic was the commander, or could you tell? If you couldn't tell, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference could be noticed, and I received confirmation from this person and the reason why the change had occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Is this person the one that you don't wish to disclose his identity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, then, leave that aside for the moment; don't take account of that. Is there anything you observed or heard from other people, other than him, that allowed you to conclude that at one point Mr. Kvocka was the commander, at another point, Mr. Meakic was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the takeover of shifts occurred, Meakic started to be present in the capacity in which Kvocka used to appear. So those differences were quite visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can you remember about what time that happened, the shift changes to Meakic from Kvocka? Just approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, nor did I know the date, but it would be in June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the document that you were asked to read parts of by Mr. Simic, let me ask you a couple of questions. Insofar as the people who did the interrogation in the administration building, did you ever observe them around other parts of the camp doing anything with the detainees, or were they, in your observations, confined to just doing interrogations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, to the best of my knowledge and according to what I saw, they were in the administration premises, that is, the premises for the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In your observation or knowledge, did you ever see, if you would have known them, members of the mine management, the Omarska mine management -- you were asked to read the portions of the document dealing with their responsibility for meals and cleaning -- did you ever see anybody that you knew to be a representative of the mine management company around the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would you have known Simo Drljaca if you saw him? I mean, was he somebody you would recognise if you saw him? The person who signed the document that you were asked about, did you know who he was? Would you have recognised him? Did you ever see him or hear that he was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you ever see him or hear that he was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You saw him at the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Once or several times?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just once. That was the most important event, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What was that event?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What was that event that you say was the most important event that he was present at?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the following event: We were lined up in lines of 30 and we had to sing, and he was present. Then we were ordered to go into the so-called canteen, the kitchen. This was an important event, very important, because that was when there was a massive beating of the detainees going in and coming out of the canteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. You told us about that. My last question is: Who gave the orders to detainees in the regular, everyday? I mean, when the detainees were told to go to lunch or to go to this building or to go to that building, or to stand up or to sit down, who were the people -- not the names of individuals -- but what kind of people were they that gave all the orders to the detainees during everyday life?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. Thank you very much. I'm sorry we have to bother you with so many little questions, but I'm sure you understand that this is the only way the process can work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. I also have a little question because most of the questions have been posed, and that is the advantage of being the last to speak. You mentioned, and you used -- regarding a visit and improvements in the camp, you mentioned that that visit was masked. Could you explain what you meant by the word "masked"? What was masked in that visit?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain, yes. I can tell you what happened. That was the first time that I saw a quarter of a loaf of bread; that was the first time I got a full plate of food. You see, I was hungry. It was the first time that I saw something like that. This was done for somebody to see that things were fine for us. That was the cosmetic improvements that I was referring to. But that was not the real state of affairs that I have had to read out to you today, without having the ability to comment on what I read. I will tell you the truth. The paper that I read, the piece of paper, it is equal to pieces of paper from the Second World War that were written in camps such as Auschwitz. They can be compared to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, has that paper got anything to do with the cosmetic improvements that I was asking you about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I was reading today simply has nothing to do with reality, not a single paragraph; it is just dead letter on paper. And they are trying with these cosmetics to persuade this Court that we were fine, and we were not fine, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are here to establish that, Witness. Witness, thank you very much for coming. You suffered certain health problems, but in any event we wish to thank you and wish you a safe journey home. The usher is now going to escort you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I saw that you were about to get on your feet, and I see you on your feet now.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is the moment. Though I had intended to raise another question regarding re-examination of witnesses, we have found a court ruling that supports our position. But the witness has left and we'll leave that for the Status Conference. But I would like to tender into evidence the statements by Edin Mrkalj, on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of April, in 1995, both of which were given after the confirmation of the indictment against Mr. Kvocka and the other accused. So I would like to tender them into evidence. Ms. Hollis was about to do so but she withdrew her proposal, so it is now our proposal that these documents be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps we could take it in the regular order for offering evidence and then we could deal with these issues, if we're now moving into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I gave the floor to Mr. Simic because he was on his feet. Let us follow the order for the offering of documents. Ms. Hollis, therefore. I think that you have some documents to tender, so please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had 3/22, which was a photograph of a man in a blue camouflage uniform, and we would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any objections on the part of the Defence? Ms. Hollis, excuse me for a moment, but I think that we also have the statements of this witness. Are you leaving that opportunity to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've already been told on the record that the Defence wishes to introduce it. If it's easier, for purposes of marking, for me to introduce it, since I've already marked it, I'll be happy to do so, if that would be easier for keeping the exhibits in order. And I would offer, then, 3/98A, which is the English version of the Office of the Prosecutor's statement taken of Edin Mrkalj on 27, 28, 29 April 1995, and 3/98B is the B/C/S version of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Simic, are there any objections to the admission of these documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that Ms. Hollis has proposed the admission -- we were out of order, so we apologise, out of turn. But I speak only on behalf of -- in my own name. We do not object to the admission of the photograph or the statement tendered by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify one thing, since we had a long discussion previously about the admission -- this is primarily directed to the Defence. I think I know your position quite well, Ms. Hollis. -- as to whether or not entire witness statements should go in or just portions that are relevant to cross-examination or completion of the impeachment process. I understand now that you're agreeing in this case to the whole statement. Well, Mr. Simic is agreeing to the whole statement. Okay. Is that correct? I just wanted to clarify that. You're happy with having the whole statement introduced? You just said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this case, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. O'Sullivan now. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On behalf of the accused Kos, we do not object to the admission of 3/22, the photo. We object to the admission of 3/98A, 98B, for the reasons stated earlier. And we renew our objection -- I will not repeat my submissions, but we renew the objection as to the admissibility of statements in their entirety. Our position is that out-of-court statements used during cross-examination are limited for impeachment purposes only. So 3/98 falls into a separate category. We object, in addition, for the reasons stated when this witness was shown the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. President, this statement does not refer and does not affect the Defence of Mr. Radic, so I should agree. But for the clarity of the proceedings, I join what Mr. O'Sullivan has said, because that transcript is our transcript. We participate in it. If Ms. Hollis at one point in time withdrew something, then she has done so for good, and that is why I support Mr. O'Sullivan in respect to that point and also in respect to statements in general. But this is not from the standpoint of the defence of Mr. Radic or Mr. Kvocka. And also, Mr. President, I will accept any ruling you may make wholeheartedly -- I want to make that clear -- whatever ruling you make in such situations, but it is a question of legal purity, if I may put it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not object to the introduction of this document into evidence by the Prosecution, but in view of the different opinions among Defence teams, and bearing in mind the fact that Ms. Hollis had withdrawn her proposal and that you will make your own ruling about that, the Defence of Zoran Zigic would suggest that the statement be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Prcac joins in the position of Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Fila, and we object to the admission of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, your response to the objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Three points, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honour, after the Prosecution indicated it would withdraw the statement, further questions were asked which, it is the Prosecution's submission, indicated that the witness misunderstood what was being asked of him in that he indicated he was being asked if he had been provided a written statement in B/C/S. The witness then went on to clarify that indeed the statement had been read to him in a language he understood and that he had certified that the statement was true and accurate as it was read to him. We believe that in that circumstance the statement can go in. The second point is this: The Prosecution offered, as a matter of keeping the procedural record clean, if you will, to offer this as the number we had marked it, 3/98A and B. Prior to that, Defence counsel for Kvocka had indeed offered the same statement to Your Honours. So that is an independent basis for allowing the statement in. Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, it was Defence counsel for Zigic who introduced the issue of the statement regarding a person by the name of Vokic. And if Your Honours review the statement, you will find that the substance of the statement deals with both Tadic and Vokic and the incident about which Defence counsel for Zigic were questioned. And Defence counsel for Zigic, who were the ones who thought the statement was important to their client, have indicated they have no objection to this statement coming in. We believe that the statement should come in, given all of those remarks that I have just made. There are three bases upon which the statement could come in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have some peace for the Judges to consult, please. Can we have a little peace, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not in a position to take a decision. Once we are complete, we will take up this discussion and consult with our colleague, Judge Fouad Riad, and we will decide then, as I don't see that the decision is important for continuing of the proceedings now. However, I would like to make a comment. I don't know why the parties who are against the admission into the record -- I'm not talking about this particular case -- are frequently the people who use those same statements. I think that we should be coherent and perhaps discuss this matter in greater depth. Either we follow the principle that what is valid is what the witness says in the courtroom and we forget everything else, or what he said before is important and we have to be consistent and accept it. To function with these double standards, I think, is rather difficult, but I leave it to you as a matter for you to think about. So that is not any instruction by the Chamber; I just wish you to think about it. I think we have to be consistent; that is all. So, Ms. Hollis, what are we going to do now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no further exhibits to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have some more?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but after that, do you have witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know if the Defence have any exhibits to offer. I believe Mr. Simic had some exhibits that he referred to. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was thinking that Mr. Simic was referring to those same statements, so I think there are no others that they wish to tender. But I do see that Mr. Tosic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to deal with this dilemma, perhaps one could say that this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What dilemma are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the admission of this statement into evidence. Because as far as I was able to understand what you said, I don't know whether you are going to agree with the proposition of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that we will decide later because Judge Fouad Riad is not present, so we'll make a decision later. Is that clear now? Ms. Hollis --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have another witness. Perhaps it's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I was thinking of that, only people were asking to speak. Yes, we'll have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Ms. Hollis, can we have the next witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, the next witness will be Sifeta Susic. I would also note for the record, Your Honours, that Mr. Daniel Saxon is at counsel table representing the Prosecutor, and Mr. Saxon will be leading the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. May we say welcome to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I'm speaking to you. You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Ms. Susic. Ms. Susic, thank you for coming here. Do you feel comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Saxon. Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Madam, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Sifeta Susic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is the date and the place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The 1st of January, 1949; Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was your place of residence until 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Up until April of 1992, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I worked in the Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Prijedor, and it is abbreviated with the letters SUP, S-U-P.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When did you commence working at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of February, 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to April 1992, approximately how many persons worked at the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Approximately 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In early 1992, who was the secretary of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In that position as secretary, did that mean that Hasan Talundzic was the highest ranking person in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was the SUP divided into different departments?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How many different departments?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: There was the crime department, the suppression and supervision of crime, where I worked; then there was the Prijedor Police Station, which included the Omarska Police Station, the Ljubija Police Station, and the Kozarac department, the traffic department; then there was the department for administration matters and the communications department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So all together was the Prijedor SUP divided into three departments?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did each of these three departments have a chief or a commander?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to the police department, was there a central police station for the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did that Prijedor Police Station have a commander?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the commander's name?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there any other police stations in the smaller towns around the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where were those?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: In Omarska, Ljubija, and the department in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did each of these police stations in the smaller communities have a commander?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who did the commanders of the police stations in Omarska, Ljubija, and Kozarac report to?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Prijedor Police Station and the chief of SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, then, was Dusko Jankovic, as commander of the Prijedor Police Station, the police commander for the entire Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With regard to the police station in Prijedor and the police stations in the smaller towns like Omarska, did those police stations have a particular internal structure?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there a commander?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How else was the structure divided?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The commander and deputy commander, and perhaps they had assistants but I'm not quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were those police stations divided into different sections?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the police station in Prijedor, whether in the town of Prijedor itself or in the smaller communities like Omarska or Kozarac, would there be a traffic section?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would there be a law enforcement section?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Perhaps I didn't understand the question properly. Were you asking me whether that structure existed in the SUP in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm speaking simply with regard to the police department itself which had an office, as you explained, in Prijedor and in the smaller communities.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So within the police stations, how were they organised in terms of their structure?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The police station of Prijedor, at the head of the station was the commander, the deputy commander, and the assistant commander. And the smaller stations, such as the Ljubija Police Station and Omarska Police Station, they had commanders or leaders and deputy leaders; I don't know whether they had assistants or whether they were termed differently. But in the Kozarac department, there was only the commander or leader of the Kozarac department, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the term "patrol sector leader"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was a patrol sector leader?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if the salary of a patrol sector leader differed from that of a regular policeman?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was the salary of a patrol sector leader higher or lower than that of an ordinary policeman?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The salaries or personal incomes were higher than the salaries of an ordinary police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if the responsibilities borne by a patrol sector leader differed from those borne by a regular policeman?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did those responsibilities differ?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, probably he had greater competencies and more complex -- his work was more complex, more responsibilities than an ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "he," Ms. Susic, are you referring to the patrol sector leader?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, in which department of the SUP did you work?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I worked in the crime department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was your supervisor in the crime department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was Ranko Mijic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What were your specific duties at the crime department in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I was the clerk for penal files, dossiers, records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And specifically, then, what would you do? What were your specific duties?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I kept records for all individuals who were sentenced for a crime and were born in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Susic, during the course of your work for those 21 years, between 1971 and 1992, did you have occasion to have personal contact with different police officers from the city of Prijedor and from nearby towns?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why would these different police officials or officers come to see you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: They would come to check data and information about certain individuals through the records we kept in the crime section so that they knew who they were dealing with, whether he had been convicted and sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that in the course of police investigative work?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During your years of service in the Prijedor SUP, what contact, if any, did you have with a police officer named Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was an employee of the police force, and any time he had to check anything on the ground or he had a request from a work organisation or institution or anything of that kind, he was duty-bound to come and see me and check out the individual, to see whether we had a file or a criminal record on that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So how often would you have these kinds of contacts with Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Endless amounts of time, whenever his work called for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever receive requests for information in writing from Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where specifically did Miroslav Kvocka work?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know, Ms. Susic, what position Miroslav Kvocka held at the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the deputy leader of the Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I'd like to ask you to look around this courtroom and tell the Judges if you can see Miroslav Kvocka here today.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Looking at it from my direction, from left to right, from the guard, he is the second in order. After the guard, the second man is Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which row are you referring to, Ms. Susic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The last row, sitting between the two guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you repeat where he's sitting again, please?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Looking at it from my angle of vision, looking at the last row, on the left-hand side, after the guard, not counting the guard, the second man in order is Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you please describe what Mr. Kvocka is wearing?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: A dark blue jacket, a light blue shirt, and a multicoloured tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please sit down now.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record please reflect that the witness has identified the defendant, Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During your years of service in the Prijedor SUP, Ms. Susic, what contact, if any, did you have with a man named Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We worked in the same department, the crime department, for the prevention of crime, in fact. Dragoljub was a crime technician, and my office, for a time, was next to that crime prevention office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So how often would you see Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Every day while I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to the war in 1992, did Mr. Prcac usually address you by your name, Sifeta?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No. He always referred to me as Siva. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, can you look around the courtroom today and tell the Judges whether you see Mr. Dragoljub Prcac present today?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He is sitting in the row before the last row, in front of the last row, where Kvocka Miroslav is sitting; and looking at it from my angle, after the guard he is the first man. You have the guard first and then Dragoljub Prcac next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "after the guard," do you mean the guard on the left or the guard on the right?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I said, from where I'm looking, on the left-hand side, moving towards the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what Mr. Prcac is wearing?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: A grey jacket with stripes, pinstripe jacket, a multicoloured tie, and a light shirt -- a patterned tie and a light shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, in general, prior to 1992, did you have good relations with your Serb and Croat colleagues in the Prijedor Police Department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, exceptionally good relations, I might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When, if ever, did your relations with your Serb colleagues in the Prijedor SUP begin to deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you observe at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: First of all, in my own service, where there were 30 employees, roughly, we lived like one family. But at the beginning of 1992 I noticed when I went into an office where there were several of my colleagues, men and women alike, Serbs, they would stop talking when I came in. They would just stop talking when I came in, and that wasn't the case previously. I felt that I was the odd man out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, you previously said that your supervisor was a man named Ranko Mijic. What was Ranko Mijic's position at the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in early 1992, what changes, if any, did you notice in the way Ranko Mijic treated you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, and I remember it well, I was going to my chief, Ranko Mijic, to sign for some post. I didn't find him. I looked for him in other offices, but the offices were closed. And one of my lady colleagues, Dzevida Jakupovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, if I can interrupt you. I'm simply asking you if you noticed a change in the way Mr. Ranko Mijic began to treat you in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, he seemed to be at a distance suddenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you normally, in the course of your daily duties, go to Ranko Mijic's office during the day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what changes, if anything, did you begin to notice in 1992 when you would go to Ranko Mijic's office?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He no longer talked in such a sympathetic way, as he had done in all the previous years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever enter your supervisor's office when Ranko Mijic was speaking with another group of people?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What changes, if any, did you observe about your treatment at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As I said, when I would enter an office, and that was frequently, they would keep quiet, they would stop talking, and you could clearly feel -- I felt that they didn't want to speak in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when you say "they," what is the ethnicity of the persons you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs, and I'm thinking about this group of people who would be in the chief's office or in the office next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So these were Serb colleagues of yours at the Prijedor SUP.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, you stated previously that in early 1992, Hasan Talundzic was the secretary of the SUP for Prijedor. Prior to assuming the position of secretary of the SUP, to your knowledge, did Hasan Talundzic have a lot of experience as a police commander or as an administrator?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he never worked in any SUP anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the Serb members of the Prijedor SUP, particularly the police force, obey the orders of Hasan Talundzic during late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: When talking to my colleague, Fikret Kadiric, who was the leader for the Travnik police, on one occasion I learned from him, he told me that Dusan Jankovic, the commander of the police station, almost daily was taking a vehicle and going off to Banja Luka, to the security centre there. He also told me that as far as he knew, he was not informing our secretary, Hasan Talundzic, of doing so, which was unthinkable previously; that is to say, before 1992, it was unthinkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, who, then, became the effective commander of the Prijedor police force at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, do you recall an occasion in early 1992 when Serb forces took over control of a television transmitter on Kozara Mountain.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall if the Prijedor Police Department undertook an investigation of that takeover of the television transmitter?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I learnt, again from Fikret ^ Kadiric, in an informal conversation, that the transmitter had allegedly been captured by a group of extremists and that a certain group of policemen, on behalf of the Prijedor SUP, was told to go to Kozara and investigate. He also told me that the group was headed by Milutin Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Milutin Vujic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, to your knowledge, were there any Muslim police officers involved in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did control of this television transmitter remain with this group of Serb extremists, as you called them, until the outbreak of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I'd like to step backwards for a moment. During your years of service in the Prijedor SUP, what contact, if any, did you have with a police officer named Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I did with the other policemen employed in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often would you have these kinds of contacts with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As required by his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would that be once a year, once a month? Can you give me some kind of an estimate?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was part of his job. Every processing, every check had to start with checking the records which I was keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What police station was Mr. Radic assigned to?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He was in the Omarska Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was this prior to the start of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I'd like to ask you to look around the courtroom once again, and can you tell the Judges whether you can see Mr. Mladjo Radic sitting here today?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The last row, as I am looking at it from the left to the right, the first man next to the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what Mr. Radic is wearing today?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He has a dark blue jacket, a light blue shirt, and a dark blue tie with some lighter coloured spots on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Susic, you worked at the Prijedor SUP until what time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Until exactly the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened prior to the 8th of April that made you decide to leave your job?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 8th of April, about 1.00 in the afternoon, I was carrying the mail to be signed by my superior, Ranko Mijic. I didn't find him in the office so I looked for him in a couple of other offices, which were also locked. My colleague Dzevida Jakupovic told me, "I'll tell you where they are but I know that that will be a cause of concern to you," and she told me that Ranko Mijic and some other colleagues of mine, inspectors and women colleagues, had gone to see Zivko Jovic to celebrate because his wife had had a baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why was this news surprising to you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: It surprised me because throughout the previous 20-year period that I had been working in the SUP, we always used to collect money and I was the person who would collect the money and buy the gift, whenever there was something to celebrate, be it a happy event, if one of our colleagues was celebrating, or if it was a tragic event, if somebody had lost a member of their family. Although I often complained and said, "Why me?" they would say, "But you will do it best." On that occasion, they didn't even ask me to contribute, as was customary, and this hurt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened later that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I waited for them, and indeed after some time, they came back. I remember Ranko Mijic was there, Zivko Jovic, Nebojsa Tomicic, Nebojsa Babic, Darinka Lujic, Nada Markovska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of this group of people that returned from the celebration?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you say at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I addressed Zivko Jovic, whom they had visited, and I asked, "Since when, Zivko, do you no longer entertain Muslims in your home?" and his answer was, "Sifeta, I didn't invite anyone. They came of their own accord." I followed my superior into the office. I put the mail on his table for him to sign; I waited. He was pale in the face and I was shaking. I was almost crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you say to your boss, Ranko Mijic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you decide to do after that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: That was close to the end of the working hours. I packed my table, cleared things away, and, like all the other employees, I went home. I couldn't sleep all night; I cried because this really did hurt me very deeply, because I finally realised that I was undesirable among this circle of people who were my friends and colleagues until the day -- until yesterday. In the morning I took the keys, reported to my boss, left the keys on his table and said I was sick. I went to see a doctor and went on sick-leave, and I never again entered SUP, except on the day when I was taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, did you make a formal request for leave from your work?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No. I was on sick-leave, and from the doctor I received the appropriate certificate testifying to my inability to work temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. After the 8th of April, 1992, when did you next have contact with someone from the Prijedor Police Department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: This may have been the 10th or the 12th or the 11th of May, I don't recollect the exact date, my boss, Ranko Mijic, called me up on the phone and told me that he had been informed by the head of the SUP, Simo Drljaca, that he should tell all non-Serb employees to come to the building of the iron ore mines, to a meeting. This building was across the street from the SUP. I answered, "Aren't you ashamed not to ask me first how I am? You know that I am sick," and I said, "I am on sick-leave now and I don't know whether I'll be able to come."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, did you go to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The new head of the SUP, Simo Drljaca, and some other persons I didn't know who were wearing military uniforms. Among my colleagues who were present, I learnt from them that they were some people from the security service centre in Banja Luka and some military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did the Serb authorities tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: They tried to persuade us, to talk to us, to convince us that we should sign loyalty to the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when you say "us," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
