utterances.text: I'm referring to employees of Muslim and Croat ethnicity who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you decide to sign this loyalty document?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Because my opinion is that even if the Muslim forces had done the same thing, if they had taken over power in such an illegal manner, I wouldn't have done that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone present signed this loyalty document?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, Nadzija Fazlic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know the ethnicity of Nadzija Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: She's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When did you subsequently see Nadzija Fazlic after that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: We met at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Nadzija Fazlic detained at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I'd like to draw your attention to the events of the 24th of June, 1992. Were you arrested on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Rade Strika came to my door that day, about 7.30. I was still in bed. He knocked on the door and he said, "Sifeta, open. It's Strika." I opened the door, and he said, "Get ready and come with me."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of Rade Strika?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Rade Strika is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there anyone else with Mr. Strika at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. A policeman called Stevo Grahovac, who was sitting in the so-called black Marica vehicle in front of my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know Mr. Grahovac's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Rade Strika's occupation, if you knew?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Strika or Mr. Grahovac tell you why they were arresting you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As I was entering the black Marica vehicle, I asked them why they were taking me, and where. And one of them -- I can't remember now who it was -- that said, "We have orders, and we don't know why. We are taking you to the SUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "the SUP," are you specifically referring to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: It was the building of the SUP, accommodating both the police station, the crime prevention department, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where specifically did these gentlemen take you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: They took me to a room behind the duty service, where I think the shift leader used to sit. It was Milenko Sormaz. He was present. I had to give him my ID card. And then he sent me outside to sit on the bench in the corridor and wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And while you were sitting on the bench in the corridor, did you see any other persons in custody at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was entering the building, in the corridor, next to the duty service room, my colleague was standing, Ago Sadikovic, who used to be the head of the department for economic crime in my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, what was Ago Sadikovic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Ago is a Muslim. Later, while I was sitting there on the bench, Nusret Sivac was brought in, another colleague of mine, who had retired a couple of years prior to that. And also taken into custody was Osman Mahmuljin, a doctor, and several other men that I didn't know, and a woman who was sitting quite close to me on another bench and who was taken together with me to the camp. And I later learnt her name was Tesma Elezovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know the ethnicity of the members of this group of people that you saw that day, apart from --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the time, how were those other prisoners or detainees dressed?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: I remember Ago Sadikovic had a leather jacket on and a striped T-shirt. I shall never forget that. Dr. Mahmuljin, Osman, had a dark blue jacket and a glittering white shirt and tie. I don't know about the others. But they were all dressed as if they had left home for half an hour and they would all be going back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you notice about the condition of these persons?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Those persons were standing there afraid and lost, just as I felt. My colleagues from work were passing by me, turning their head away from me, whereas I looked them all straight in the eye, because I had nothing to fear. But this was terribly painful, having been so close, such good friends with so many people for so many years and they refused to look at you. At one point in time, someone said that we were going out into the corridor, the yard behind the SUP building. I went too, but Rade Strika, from the steps, from the first or second floor, called out, "Not you, Sifeta. You come back." Only the men were taken out. I stayed in that corridor until 2.00. At about 2.00 -- there was a clock on the wall, and that is how I know it was roughly 2.00 -- Grahovac said, "Come with me." And the woman whose name I later learnt as Elezovic, the two of us went into the yard of the SUP building and there was that same black Marica parked, and the men were being taken out of a room that was used as a detention, for remand detention. Those men had been in quite a normal condition an hour before. They came out black and blue, torn, bloodied. It was terrible to look at. I was pushed into the back part of the black Marica and Stevo Grahovac told the two of us to go and sit next to the doctor. I quietly asked Stevo, "Where are you taking us?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was his response?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: He said, "To Omarska."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can just take you back for a moment. When you refer to the men coming out of the room who were in a beaten condition, are you referring to Ago Sadikovic, Nusret Sivac, and the doctor Osman Mahmuljin, who you had seen in the corridor previously?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And other men whose names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the vehicle in which you were in pass through any towns on the way to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the vehicle Tomo Stojakovic was also with us -- he's a policeman -- and another man. I know him by the name of Bato. As far as I remember, we went to elementary school together. We first went to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was: Did the vehicle that you were in pass through any towns that you recall on the way to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I just wanted to explain things in a little greater detail. We passed through Kozarac on the Prijedor to Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you notice about the condition of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Actually, it's not the centre of Kozarac. The road is the Prijedor to Banja Luka road. But the houses of that settlement that were next to this main road were all destroyed and just the brick skeletons remained. The roofs were burned down, the windows. It was a terrible sight to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time was there any discussion inside the vehicle that you recall?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No. Even if there was, I was so upset that I wouldn't have heard or understood anything. I was in a state of shock almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately what time of day did you arrive at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: If we left about 2.00 -- I can't remember exactly. It was in the afternoon. Whether it was 3.00 or 4.00 -- I don't know how long the drive takes from Prijedor to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, met you at the entrance to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: The vehicle, the black Marica, stopped in front of the restaurant. When I got out, Miroslav Kvocka was standing there, my colleague, as I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall how Miroslav Kvocka was dressed at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was wearing a camouflage suit, uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Miroslav Kvocka say to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Another man was standing there, dressed in the same uniform. Miroslav said to him, "Return the IDs to these two women and take them immediately to the restaurant."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the other man do what Miroslav Kvocka had told him to do?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that other man?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just know that he had a dark complexion. He was dark-skinned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if that other man had a nickname of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Later I heard that they called him either Kole or Krle, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did this man known as Krle or Kole escort you to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as this man escorted you to the restaurant, what happened to the other passengers who had been with you in the van that brought you to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: As soon as we got out of the police van, the men were immediately ordered, because there were several other soldiers or guards, or men anyway, there present, they ordered them to lean against the wall of the restaurant with their arms spread out and their palms leaning on the wall, and they beat them immediately. It was a second that I stayed there but they started the beating straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, how far away at that moment was Miroslav Kvocka from the persons who were being beaten against the wall?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: That was right there, straight away. The police van was a couple of metres away from the wall of the restaurant, and they were all standing there. They were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How far away was Miroslav Kvocka from the men who were being beaten, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Several metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time, did Miroslav Kvocka say anything to the persons who were performing the beating?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear him say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As the man known as Krle or Kole escorted you to the restaurant area, can you describe what you saw, what you remember?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that infamous pista where people were sitting with their heads bowed between their knees. It was a dreadful sight. They hardly looked like human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, do you have any idea how many men were sitting on the pista that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Very many, but I can't give you a number. A hundred, more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you recall, were the men on the pista moving at all?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: No. The moment that it took me to pass from the police van to the entrance of the restaurant, I didn't notice. This was a very short glance that I cast in that direction. But it was a frightening sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the temperature like on that afternoon in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: It was extremely hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point did you eventually enter the restaurant area?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who, if anyone, did you see inside the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Women were there already; I don't know how many, maybe 20 or 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of these women?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Jadranka Cigelj, whom I knew personally, who approached me immediately because I was crying terribly. I was terrified. She consoled me. She whispered, "You'll manage. Look at the rest of us. We're still alive. So you must bear out, as we have. You have to."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see by the clock that we have passed 2.30. This would be a logical breaking point for me with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon, we are going to accept your logic to adjourn. We are going to have a very long weekend which will be welcome for all of us to have a rest, but also for the witness. I wish you a pleasant weekend, and we'll meet again on Tuesday, at 9.30. As you know, there will be no hearings on Thursday and Friday, only Tuesday and Wednesday, so that everybody knows and that you may plan your own lives as well. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned. Excuse me. I would like the witness to leave first

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are now going to adjourn. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.33 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
